Fermented foods for beginners

Fermented foods are among the oldest ways to keep vegetables through the winter. A jar, salt and patience are enough to start: shredded cabbage packed under its own brine turns into sauerkraut in about three weeks at room temperature, and the flavour keeps changing for months in a cool cellar.

The salt matters more than most recipes admit. Two percent of the weight of the vegetables is a good default; less invites soft, slimy batches, more slows the lactic bacteria down. Weigh the cabbage after trimming it, not before, and use salt without iodine or anti-caking agents.

Keeping the vegetables under the brine

Anything that floats above the brine can grow mould. A small glass weight, a clean stone or a freezer bag filled with brine keeps the vegetables down. Check the jar every few days during the first week and push the vegetables back under if the brine level drops. See the guide to fermentation weights for the options and this broken link for nothing at all.

Taste the batch every week; stop when you like it, not when the recipe says so.

Once the taste is right, move the jar to the fridge. Cold slows the fermentation almost to a stop, and a well made batch keeps for half a year. Kimchi, pickled cucumbers and fermented hot sauce all follow the same rules with different vegetables and spices.
